title: [Mathematics] Exponential Growth: Doubling, Decay and Logarithms
summary: Build exponential models from repeated multiplication. Original storage and workshop examples develop percentage factors, doubling and half-life, inverse changes, recurrences, negative and fractional exponents, logarithms, continuous rates, geometric means, graph scales and capacity limits. Five recall questions with answers and a paper or spreadsheet storage exercise. Primary mathematical reading: OpenStax, College Algebra 1e chapters hosted by LibreTexts, CC BY 4.0. Original dialogue and cases, no textbook figures or quotations. https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Algebra/College_Algebra_1e_(OpenStax)/06:_Exponential_and_Logarithmic_Functions/6.02:_Exponential_Functions https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Algebra/College_Algebra_1e_(OpenStax)/06:_Exponential_and_Logarithmic_Functions/6.04:_Logarithmic_Functions https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Algebra/College_Algebra_1e_(OpenStax)/06:_Exponential_and_Logarithmic_Functions/6.06:_Logarithmic_Properties License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
instructions: Begin with adding twenty versus increasing twenty percent. Assume no prior algebra reading. Both ash and sage teach developed examples and contrasts. Distinguish discrete rounds from smooth model extensions, factor from percentage rate, percentage points from relative changes, and endpoint-equivalent rates from actual paths. Keep units and model limits explicit. Avoid promised financial returns or claims that human skills compound at fixed rates. Preserve five seven-second recall pauses followed by answers.

turns.t: A digital archive starts with one hundred files. One copying rule adds twenty files every round. Another increases the existing count by twenty percent every round. After one round, both archives contain one hundred and twenty files. That first result hides the difference. After the second round, the first archive contains one hundred and forty, while the second contains one hundred and forty-four. After the third, the first contains one hundred and sixty, while the second model gives one hundred and seventy-two point eight. The rules began together, then separated because one repeatedly adds and the other repeatedly multiplies.

turns.t: The fractional file count tells us to state what this example represents. We are using an ideal mathematical model of archive size, which could be measured in units of storage, rather than an exact procedure for counting indivisible files. With real file counts we would need rounding rules or a probabilistic model. For now, call the starting quantity one hundred storage units. The comparison becomes clean. Adding twenty units each round gives linear growth. Multiplying the latest amount by one point two gives exponential growth. The distinction is the rule, not whether the numbers look impressive.

turns.t: A twenty-percent increase means keeping the whole current amount and adding one fifth of that same amount. One hundred percent plus twenty percent is one hundred and twenty percent, expressed as the multiplier one point two. That multiplier is often called the growth factor. The rate is twenty percent per round. The factor is one point two per round. Confusing them would be disastrous: multiplying by zero point two would retain only twenty percent and discard eighty percent. The original amount remains part of an increase calculation.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: After the first round, the twenty-percent rule adds twenty-four units because it acts on one hundred and twenty. After the next, it adds twenty-eight point eight because it acts on one hundred and forty-four. The percentage stays fixed while the absolute addition grows. In the linear archive, the addition stays fixed while its percentage of the growing total becomes smaller. Twenty units is twenty percent of one hundred, but only ten percent of two hundred. The two descriptions answer different questions about the same change.

turns.t: This lesson develops the mathematics behind those rules: repeated multiplication, doubling times, decay, logarithms and scales that show ratios. We will use original storage, workshop and token examples. They are mathematical cases, not forecasts about an actual business or claims that human skill improves at a fixed percentage each day. Exponential models are useful precisely when the same proportional rule keeps applying over comparable intervals. If the process changes, the calculation needs to change with it. No prior algebra lesson is needed; we will build the notation from the operations.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Imagine writing one point two multiplied by one point two multiplied by one point two. Exponent notation compresses that repeated multiplication. We say one point two to the third power. The base is one point two, and the exponent is three. For our archive, multiply that power by the starting hundred. After three rounds, the quantity is one hundred times one point two cubed. The exponent counts how many times the factor has acted. It is not a command to multiply the base by three.

turns.t: That difference can be heard in a simpler example. Two to the fifth power means two times two times two times two times two, which is thirty-two. Two times five is ten. Both use the numbers two and five, but they describe different operations. When the exponent is a positive whole number, counting repeated factors is enough. Zero, negative and fractional exponents will extend the same structure later. The extension is useful because we may want to describe the starting time, work backward, or ask what a smooth model predicts between full rounds.

turns.t: At round zero, no change has happened. The quantity must still equal the starting hundred. That is why any nonzero base raised to the zero power is one in this system. One hundred times one equals one hundred. This is consistent with the exponent rule that removing one multiplication divides by the base. One point two squared divided by one point two gives one point two to the first power. Divide again and get one, corresponding to the zero power. The notation preserves the relationship between successive steps.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: We can describe a general positive exponential model in spoken form: current amount equals initial amount multiplied by a fixed factor raised to the number of intervals. The initial amount sets the overall scale. The factor sets the proportional change. The interval tells us what one step means. Ten percent per day is not ten percent per month. If a model uses days, entering a count of months without conversion changes the question. A growth rate without its time interval is missing essential information, even if the percentage is written very precisely.

turns.t: The first recall question is this. Two quantities both start at one hundred. One adds twenty each round, and the other grows by twenty percent each round. Why do they agree after the first round but differ after the second?

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: At the first round, twenty percent of the starting hundred is twenty, so both reach one hundred and twenty. In the next round, the fixed addition is still twenty, while twenty percent of the new amount is twenty-four. The totals become one hundred and forty and one hundred and forty-four. Linear growth keeps an absolute difference constant. Exponential growth keeps a ratio constant over equal intervals. The first matching step does not establish that the underlying processes are the same.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Now imagine we have a table rather than a stated rule. One sequence reads fifty, seventy-five, one hundred and twelve point five, and one hundred and sixty-eight point seven five. The differences are twenty-five, thirty-seven point five, and fifty-six point two five. They are not equal. But dividing each value by its predecessor gives one point five every time. That is consistent with fifty-percent growth each interval. To recognize an exponential pattern, ratios are often more revealing than differences. The intervals must be equal for that direct comparison to make sense.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: A second table reads fifty, seventy-five, one hundred, one hundred and twenty-five. Its successive differences are all twenty-five. Its ratios are one point five, then about one point three three, then one point two five. That pattern is linear rather than exponential. The first two entries match the earlier table exactly. Two observations alone cannot establish which rule generated them. A process description or additional observations helps distinguish the possibilities. This is a specific mathematical limitation: many functions can pass through the same two points.

turns.t: A curve can also rise rapidly without being exponential. The square of time gives one, four, nine and sixteen when time is one, two, three and four. The increments grow, so the curve bends upward. Yet the ratios do not stay constant over those equal intervals. This is quadratic growth, with the variable serving as the base and a fixed exponent of two. Exponential growth places the variable in the exponent of a fixed base. A steep graph is not a definition. The repeated relationship between input and output matters.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: There is a useful long-run mathematical result behind the excitement about exponentials. A positive exponential with a factor greater than one eventually outgrows any fixed positive power of time, even when its early values are smaller. But eventually can be far beyond the period that matters in an application. A large linear starting amount can remain larger than a small exponential quantity for many steps. And a real process may encounter limits long before a theoretical crossover. The mathematical comparison is about indefinitely extended functions, not a guarantee about physical systems.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Consider two original storage plans. Plan A starts at one thousand units and adds one hundred per month. Plan B starts at one hundred units and doubles each month. After three months, A has one thousand three hundred and B has eight hundred. After four months, A has one thousand four hundred and B has one thousand six hundred. The smaller initial amount has overtaken the larger one under those rules. We found the crossing by checking steps. The fact that B eventually wins does not mean it was larger from the beginning.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: For the doubling plan, each step has a fixed ratio of two. Going from one hundred to two hundred takes one month. Going from two hundred to four hundred also takes one month. Going from four hundred to eight hundred takes another. The absolute increases become larger, but the doubling time remains the same. More generally, a constant-rate positive exponential has a constant doubling time when it grows, or a constant half-life when it decays. Those times describe proportional change rather than a fixed number of units added or removed.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: If a process doubles every three hours, six hours produce two doublings, so the factor is four. Nine hours produce three doublings, so the factor is eight. Twelve hours produce four doublings, so the factor is sixteen. It would be wrong to say that twelve hours gives a factor of four simply because twelve contains four groups of three. Four is the number of doublings, not the resulting multiplier. Repeated doubling means raising two to that count. Time divided by doubling time supplies the exponent.

turns.t: That lets us write a model without first knowing a percentage rate. Suppose the starting amount is forty units and the doubling time is three hours. At time twelve hours, the amount is forty times two to the fourth power, or six hundred and forty. The same model at six hours gives one hundred and sixty. If the starting amount changes to eighty while the doubling time stays the same, every predicted amount doubles. The shape in relative terms stays the same, while the scale changes.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Now reverse the process. Start with six hundred and forty units and retain half every three hours. After three hours, three hundred and twenty remain. After six, one hundred and sixty remain. After nine, eighty remain. After twelve, forty remain. This is exponential decay. The amount removed in each interval decreases: first three hundred and twenty, then one hundred and sixty, then eighty. The proportion removed is constant. If instead we removed one hundred units every three hours, that would be linear decline until some rule changed at zero.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: A pure positive exponential decay model approaches zero without reaching it at any finite time. Repeatedly multiplying a positive number by a positive factor less than one still leaves a positive number. That does not mean an actual count of individual objects can contain a fraction forever. It means the smooth mathematical model has that property. A physical measurement may also fall below detection long before the modeled quantity is exactly zero. A threshold such as less than one unit is a different question from exact mathematical disappearance.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: A twenty-percent reduction uses the factor zero point eight. Start at five hundred units. The next amounts are four hundred, three hundred and twenty, and two hundred and fifty-six. The losses are one hundred, eighty and sixty-four. Each reduction is twenty percent of what remains at that step. After three reductions, the retained fraction is zero point eight cubed, or zero point five one two. Therefore fifty-one point two percent of the original remains. Removing twenty percent three times does not remove sixty percent of the initial amount.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: The second recall question: a quantity retains eighty percent of its current amount each round. It begins at five hundred. What remains after three rounds, and why is subtracting three lots of one hundred the wrong operation?

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Two hundred and fifty-six remains. Multiply five hundred by zero point eight three times. The first reduction is one hundred, but the next is eighty and the next is sixty-four because the base amount has shrunk. Subtracting one hundred each time would describe a fixed absolute removal, which is a different rule. Repeated percentage changes act on the current amount unless the problem explicitly defines them against some other reference amount.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: That changing reference explains a common percentage trap. Increase a quantity by twenty percent, then decrease the result by twenty percent. Starting from one hundred, the first step gives one hundred and twenty. The second removes twenty-four, leaving ninety-six. The combined factor is one point two times zero point eight, or zero point nine six. The equal-looking percentages do not cancel because the decrease is taken from a larger base. Reversing the order also produces ninety-six in this simple multiplication-only case.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: To undo a twenty-percent increase exactly, divide by one point two. The required multiplier is about zero point eight three three three. That corresponds to a decrease of sixteen and two thirds percent from the increased amount. Conversely, to recover from a twenty-percent decrease, multiply by one point two five, which is a twenty-five-percent increase. The original and final quantities determine the ratio. Naming the percentage without naming its reference can make the same numerical movement sound contradictory when it is actually consistent.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: We can make the same point with a nonfinancial workshop example. A machine's processing time falls from ten minutes to eight minutes per item. That is a twenty-percent reduction in time. Its ideal processing rate rises from six items per hour to seven point five items per hour. That is a twenty-five-percent increase in rate, assuming continuous operation with no other delays. Time per item and items per time are reciprocals. The percentage change in one is not simply the same percentage with an opposite sign in the other.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: There is another distinction between percentages and percentage points. Suppose a fictional completion rate rises from twenty percent to thirty percent. It rises by ten percentage points. Relative to the original twenty percent, it rises by fifty percent because ten divided by twenty is one half. Saying it rose ten percent would normally mean multiplying twenty percent by one point one, giving twenty-two percent. These descriptions are not interchangeable. The denominator in a relative-change calculation carries part of the meaning, whether we are discussing rates, proportions or ordinary quantities.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Now consider two successive increases of ten percent. Their combined factor is one point one squared, or one point two one. The total increase is twenty-one percent. The extra one percent comes from applying the second increase to the first increase as well as to the starting amount. We can derive it without a calculator: multiply one plus one tenth by one plus one tenth. The result has one, two tenths and one hundredth. The cross term is small for small percentages, which helps explain why simply adding rates sometimes looks close while still being inexact.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: If successive percentage changes differ, multiply their factors. A ten-percent increase followed by a five-percent decrease gives one point one times zero point nine five, or one point zero four five. The final amount is four point five percent above the original. Adding ten and negative five would predict five percent, slightly too high. For long chains, those differences can accumulate. You can keep a running product of factors, but do not round heavily after every step if you want an accurate final result.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Order has a precise role here. Multiplying by one point one and then by zero point nine five gives the same endpoint as doing those two multiplications in reverse order. Multiplication of those factors is commutative. However, the intermediate values differ. And if a fixed amount is added or removed between changes, the endpoint can depend on order. Starting at one hundred, adding twenty then doubling gives two hundred and forty. Doubling then adding twenty gives two hundred and twenty. A system with additions and multipliers needs its sequence specified.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: This matters for an archive that both grows proportionally and receives new material. Suppose it starts at one hundred units, grows by ten percent during each round, and receives twenty new units at the end of each round. The first result is one hundred and thirty. The second is one hundred and sixty-three. The third is one hundred and ninety-nine point three. That is not simply one hundred times one point one cubed, because each added batch has its own time to grow. The repeated rule combines multiplication with an addition.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: We can account for the third-round total by following the batches. The original hundred has grown for three rounds, becoming one hundred and thirty-three point one. The first added twenty has grown for two rounds, becoming twenty-four point two. The second added twenty has grown for one round, becoming twenty-two. The final twenty is added at the end and has not grown yet. Add those four contributions and get one hundred and ninety-nine point three. This batch view explains the recurrence rather than asking us to memorize a formula blindly.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: The decay version produces another surprising result. Imagine a container with one hundred abstract tokens, losing ten percent of its current amount each round, then receiving ten new tokens. After the loss it has ninety, and after the addition it is back at one hundred. That amount is an equilibrium for the rule. If it starts at fifty, the next amount is fifty-five. If it starts at one hundred and fifty, the next is one hundred and forty-five. The same process can pull amounts toward a stable level rather than toward zero or infinity.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Why one hundred? At equilibrium, the ten-percent loss must equal the fixed ten-token addition. Ten percent of one hundred is ten. More generally, divide the fixed addition by the fractional loss to find the balance in this particular recurrence. The difference from the equilibrium shrinks by the retention factor each round. Starting at fifty gives a deficit of fifty; after one round the deficit is forty-five. That is exponential decay of the deviation even though the total quantity is increasing. Always identify which quantity follows the exponential rule.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: We now have a reason to work backward. Suppose a quantity grows by a factor of one point five per interval and later measures three hundred and thirty-seven point five. What was it three intervals earlier? Divide by one point five three times. The earlier amount was one hundred. In exponent notation, multiplying by one point five to the negative third power means exactly that repeated division. A negative exponent does not mean the quantity becomes negative. It means taking the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: For a factor of two, two to the negative first power is one half. Two to the negative second power is one quarter. Two to the negative third power is one eighth. The pattern lets the same exponential expression describe times before the chosen reference point. But choosing a negative time in an algebraic model does not establish that the modeled process really existed that far back. If the archive was created yesterday, a smooth mathematical extension to last year is not a historical account. The formula has a mathematical domain and an application domain.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Fractional exponents answer a different question. If a smooth model doubles over one full interval, what multiplier over half an interval would be consistent with two identical half-interval steps? Call the unknown multiplier something that, when multiplied by itself, gives two. That is the square root of two, approximately one point four one four. It corresponds to an increase of about forty-one point four percent over the half interval. Fifty percent would be wrong because one point five squared is two point two five, which exceeds the required full-interval factor of two.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: The same logic applies to converting monthly and yearly factors. If a hypothetical quantity increases by ten percent every month for twelve months, its annual factor is one point one to the twelfth power, approximately three point one three eight. That is an increase of about two hundred and thirteen point eight percent over the year. If instead the annual increase is ten percent, the consistent monthly factor is the twelfth root of one point one, approximately one point zero zero seven nine seven four. That is roughly zero point eight percent per month, not ten percent divided into an identical whole-number rule without compounding.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: These are mathematical rate conversions, not promised returns or product terms. Different applications define stated rates in different ways. The wording must establish whether a rate is effective over the whole interval or a nominal rate split into subintervals. A percentage label cannot tell you that by itself. In pure mathematics, a specified factor over a specified time is enough to derive an equivalent constant factor over another time. In a real contract or scientific process, you must first establish that those are actually the intended quantities.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Suppose our archive reaches four times its original size. A doubling rule needs two intervals because two squared is four. To reach eight times the original, it needs three. To reach sixteen times, it needs four. We have been answering the question, what exponent produces this multiplier? A logarithm gives that question a name. The logarithm base two of eight is three because two to the third power is eight. The logarithm is the exponent we need, not a mysterious extra operation unrelated to the growth process.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: The third recall question: what does the logarithm base two of sixteen mean, and why is its value four rather than eight?

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: It asks what power of two equals sixteen. Four factors of two multiply to sixteen, so the answer is four. Dividing sixteen by two gives eight, but that answers a different question. Logarithms undo exponentiation by finding the exponent. Division undoes one multiplication. Keeping those operations separate is what lets us solve for the number of growth intervals rather than merely undoing a single interval.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Base ten gives especially familiar examples. Ten to the first power is ten, so the base-ten logarithm of ten is one. Ten squared is one hundred, so the logarithm of one hundred is two. Ten cubed is one thousand, so the logarithm of one thousand is three. The logarithm of one is zero because ten to the zero power is one. The logarithm of one tenth is negative one because ten to the negative first power is one tenth. A negative logarithm can therefore describe a perfectly ordinary positive fraction.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: For real logarithms with a positive base other than one, the input must be positive. There is no real exponent that makes a positive base equal zero or a negative number. That restriction follows from the exponential function we are reversing. It is not an arbitrary calculator complaint. The base also cannot be one because every power of one is one, so it would not provide a unique inverse. We will stay with real-number logarithms here; complex-number extensions are a different subject.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Logarithms need not be whole numbers. The base-two logarithm of ten lies between three and four because two cubed is eight and two to the fourth is sixteen. A calculator gives about three point three two two. That means a smooth doubling model requires about three point three two two doubling intervals to grow by a factor of ten. If the process changes only at discrete whole rounds, the first round at or above tenfold is round four. The smooth crossing time and the first whole-round threshold are different answers to different questions.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Return to growth of twenty percent per round. We want to know when a starting amount doubles. The factor after an unknown number of rounds is one point two raised to that number. We need that factor to equal two. The answer is the logarithm base one point two of two, approximately three point eight zero two rounds in the smooth extension. At three full rounds the factor is one point seven two eight. At four it is two point zero seven three six. Therefore the first whole round at or above double is the fourth.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: A calculator often supplies base-ten logarithms and natural logarithms, rather than a button for every possible base. The change-of-base rule solves that problem. The logarithm base one point two of two equals the natural logarithm of two divided by the natural logarithm of one point two. We could use base-ten logarithms in both numerator and denominator and get the same result. The chosen common base cancels out in the ratio. What must remain consistent is using the same logarithm base on both parts.

turns.i: Teach naturally and precisely, with both voices contributing explanations. Speak factors, rates and time units distinctly. All storage and token cases are hypothetical mathematical models. Preserve five recall pauses.
turns.t: Here is why that rule works. Let the unknown exponent be the number of rounds. One point two to that exponent equals two. Taking logarithms turns the exponent into a multiplier: the number of rounds times the logarithm of one point two equals the logarithm of two. Divide by the logarithm of one point two to isolate the number of rounds. We are not dividing the original amounts two and one point two. We are dividing their logarithms because the unknown occupied an exponent.

turns.t: The natural logarithm uses a particular base called e, approximately two point seven one eight two eight. This number appears naturally when growth is modeled as continuous and its instantaneous rate is proportional to its current size. You can use natural logarithms without deriving calculus first, just as you can use square roots before studying advanced geometry. The important relationship here is that e raised to the natural logarithm of a positive number returns that number. Natural logarithm and exponential with base e undo each other.

turns.t: A continuous model is often written as initial amount times e raised to a rate constant times elapsed time. The rate constant must match the time unit. If time is measured in hours, the constant is per hour. A positive constant gives growth and a negative one gives decay. The factor over one hour is e raised to that constant. This distinguishes an instantaneous proportional rate constant from an effective percentage change across a whole hour. They are close when small, but they are not exactly identical.

turns.t: For example, a continuous rate constant of zero point one per hour produces a one-hour factor of e to zero point one, approximately one point one zero five one seven. That is about ten point five two percent growth over the hour. Conversely, an exact ten-percent increase per hour corresponds to a continuous rate constant equal to the natural logarithm of one point one, approximately zero point zero nine five three one per hour. Both descriptions can represent the same curve when converted correctly. Mixing their numerical rates without conversion describes different curves.

turns.t: The doubling time of a continuous growth model is the natural logarithm of two divided by its positive rate constant. The natural logarithm of two is approximately zero point six nine three. For a rate constant of zero point one per hour, the doubling time is about six point nine three hours. The starting amount cancels out. A quantity beginning at ten and one beginning at ten thousand both double in the same time if they share the same constant proportional growth rule. They do not gain the same number of units.

turns.t: For a decay factor of zero point eight per round, the half-life in the smooth extension is the natural logarithm of one half divided by the natural logarithm of zero point eight. Both logarithms are negative, so the ratio is positive. The answer is approximately three point one zero six rounds. After three complete rounds, fifty-one point two percent remains. After four, forty point nine six percent remains. The first complete round below half is therefore the fourth. The signs and neighboring whole-round values both help interpret the result.

turns.t: A useful approximation connects small percentage rates to doubling time. For a small fractional increase r per interval, the natural logarithm of one plus r is close to r. The exact doubling time is the natural logarithm of two divided by the natural logarithm of one plus r. Replacing the denominator by r gives about zero point six nine three divided by r. Written with the rate as a percentage number, that is roughly sixty-nine point three divided by the percentage. It is an approximation, and its error grows as the rate becomes larger.

turns.t: At one percent per interval, that approximation gives about sixty-nine point three intervals, while the exact value is about sixty-nine point six six. At twenty percent, the approximation gives about three point four seven intervals, while the exact value is about three point eight zero two. The error is more noticeable. The popular rule of seventy uses a nearby convenient numerator, but it does not replace an exact logarithm calculation when precision matters. A remembered shortcut is most useful when its assumptions travel with it.

turns.t: Logarithms also turn multiplication into addition. The base-two logarithm of eight is three, and the base-two logarithm of four is two. Their product is thirty-two, whose base-two logarithm is five. Three plus two equals five because multiplying powers of the same base adds their exponents. This is the product rule for logarithms. It applies to positive inputs. It explains why logarithms are useful for long chains of growth factors: the logarithm of the combined factor is the sum of the logarithms of the individual factors.

turns.t: Division becomes subtraction for the same reason. The logarithm of eight divided by four is the logarithm of two, which is one in base two. Subtract the logarithm of four from the logarithm of eight and get three minus two, again one. Raising a positive quantity to a power becomes multiplication of its logarithm by that power. These relationships all follow from exponent rules. They are not independent tricks pasted onto the subject. Each lets us rearrange a problem involving repeated multiplication into a simpler problem involving sums or products.

turns.t: But the logarithm of a sum is not the sum of the logarithms. Eight plus four is twelve. Its base-two logarithm is between three and four, whereas the logarithms of eight and four add to five. Five is the logarithm of their product, thirty-two. A rule that works for products cannot be transferred to sums just because the expressions look similar. In the archive with added batches, this distinction is why taking a logarithm does not instantly turn the entire expression into one simple straight line.

turns.t: The fourth recall question: why can logarithms turn a product of growth factors into a sum, but not generally turn a sum of quantities into a sum of their logarithms?

turns.t: Multiplying powers with the same base adds their exponents, and logarithms recover those exponents. That gives the product rule. Addition does not have the corresponding exponent rule. For example, eight times four is thirty-two, so their base-two logarithms add to five. Eight plus four is twelve, whose base-two logarithm is not five. The algebra follows the operation being performed. Replacing a product with a sum changes the mathematical structure and invalidates that particular shortcut.

turns.t: Now imagine plotting archive size vertically against time horizontally. On an ordinary linear vertical axis, equal distances represent equal additions: perhaps one hundred units between every marked line. An exponential curve bends upward as the increases grow. On a logarithmic vertical axis, equal distances represent equal ratios instead. A base-ten scale might mark one, ten, one hundred and one thousand at equally spaced positions. Each step multiplies by ten. The scale compresses a large range while preserving the meaning of proportional comparisons.

turns.t: On that logarithmic vertical axis, a positive exponential with a constant factor becomes a straight line against ordinary time. Taking the logarithm of initial amount times factor to the time gives the logarithm of the initial amount plus time multiplied by the logarithm of the factor. That has the form of a straight line: starting height plus a constant slope times time. The slope represents proportional growth, expressed through the logarithm of the factor. A flat line would represent an unchanged quantity, not slow exponential growth hidden by the display.

turns.t: This can help compare two quantities with very different sizes. Suppose one grows from ten to twenty while another grows from one thousand to two thousand. Both double. On a linear axis, the second change is much larger vertically because its absolute increase is larger. On a logarithmic axis, the two changes occupy equal vertical distances because their ratios are equal. Neither display is inherently dishonest. They emphasize different relationships. The axis label tells you which interpretation is appropriate, and a meaningful comparison requires reading it.

turns.t: A logarithmic axis also cannot display zero or negative values in the ordinary real-number form we have described. If a chart includes such values, it needs a different transformation or special treatment. A line that visually approaches the bottom of a log chart is not necessarily approaching zero on a linear scale. The bottom may be one, one tenth or another positive cutoff. Without knowing the labeled values, visual height alone does not reveal the underlying amount. The transformation changes how distances map to quantities.

turns.t: There is another kind of logarithmic graph with both axes transformed. On a log-log plot, a power law such as area proportional to length squared becomes a straight line. Its slope reflects the exponent two. On a plot with only the vertical axis logarithmic, an exponential in ordinary time becomes straight. These are different arrangements. Seeing a straight line on a graph with logarithmic labels is not enough to declare exponential growth. You need to know which axes are transformed and which variables they represent.

turns.t: We can derive the power-law case from a square. If its side length doubles, its area becomes four times as large. If the side triples, area becomes nine times as large. Area equals side length squared, so the logarithm of area equals twice the logarithm of side length, apart from any unit-related reference constant. Equal logarithmic steps in length give twice as many logarithmic steps in area. In an exponential model, by contrast, equal ordinary time steps give equal logarithmic changes in amount. The transformed coordinate on the horizontal axis makes the distinction.

turns.t: For measurements with units, it is helpful to think of logarithms as acting on ratios to a reference quantity. The ratio is dimensionless. Changing the unit used to report a raw measurement should not change the underlying physical relationship. For our archive, we can plot the logarithm of current size divided by initial size. At the starting point the ratio is one, so its logarithm is zero. A doubling takes the ratio to two regardless of whether storage is measured in bytes or another consistent unit. Ratios remove the arbitrary scale factor.

turns.t: Logarithms give another answer to a familiar averaging problem. Suppose a quantity increases by fifty percent in one interval and falls by fifty percent in the next. Its factors are one point five and zero point five, whose product is zero point seven five. The arithmetic average of the percentage changes is zero, but the final quantity is twenty-five percent below the starting amount. An equivalent constant factor over the two intervals is the square root of zero point seven five, approximately zero point eight six six. That is a decrease of about thirteen point four percent per interval.

turns.t: This equivalent factor is a geometric mean. For positive factors, multiply them and take the root corresponding to the number of intervals. With two factors, use a square root. With three, use a cube root. The resulting constant factor reproduces the same endpoint when repeated for the same number of intervals. It does not reproduce the intermediate path. The path with a large rise followed by a large fall can have consequences that a smooth decline does not, even if their beginning and ending values match.

turns.t: Logarithms make the geometric mean easy to interpret: take the logarithm of each positive factor, average those logarithms, then reverse the logarithm. In a product, the logs add. Dividing their sum by the number of intervals gives the log of the equivalent repeated factor. This is why an average appropriate for additive changes can fail for multiplicative changes. The operation that builds the total determines the meaningful way to summarize the sequence. There is no single average that answers every question about variation.

turns.t: Suppose a quantity goes from one hundred to one hundred and forty-four over two equal intervals, but we do not know the intermediate value. A constant exponential model would use the square root of one point four four as its factor, which is one point two. That gives twenty percent per interval and an intermediate value of one hundred and twenty. It is one model consistent with the endpoints. The actual path could instead go to two hundred before falling to one hundred and forty-four. The equivalent rate describes the endpoints without proving the path.

turns.t: An endpoint ratio over many intervals can also conceal a change in mechanism. A copying process might expand quickly at first, then stop because storage fills. Averaging across the whole period may produce a modest equivalent rate that never describes any individual phase well. A model can fit a pair of measurements perfectly while failing between them or beyond them. In a practical analysis, plotting the intermediate values and understanding the process can reveal whether a fixed factor is reasonable over the interval being used.

turns.t: Even a small difference between assumed factors can become large when repeated. Compare one point zero two and one point zero three over twenty intervals. Their ratio after twenty intervals is one point zero three divided by one point zero two, all raised to the twentieth power. That is about one point two one five, so the second endpoint is about twenty-one point five percent larger. The rates differed by only one percentage point per interval. Repetition amplifies the difference between the assumptions without making either assumption more credible.

turns.t: The starting amount and the factor affect predictions differently. A ten-percent error in the initial amount creates a ten-percent error in every later prediction if the factor is correct. An error in the factor compounds with the number of intervals. This is why long-horizon exponential forecasts can be extremely sensitive to a small rate error. The algebra is exact conditional on the inputs. It does not remove uncertainty about those inputs or establish that a rate will remain fixed. A useful forecast must distinguish mathematical propagation from knowledge about the process.

turns.t: A real growth mechanism can change because resources, space or participants are limited. In a simple bounded-growth picture, the proportional growth rate becomes smaller as the quantity approaches a capacity. That can create a curve that begins approximately exponential, then bends toward a ceiling. We do not need to claim every real process follows one particular bounded equation. The concrete point is that continued proportional growth requires the conditions supporting that growth to persist. A successful early exponential fit is not evidence that those conditions can persist indefinitely.

turns.t: Our archive makes this visible without a biological or economic claim. If the available storage is one thousand units, a mathematical rule predicting two thousand stored units cannot describe the same physical arrangement unless capacity changes, old material is removed, or the counting definition changes. Something must give. We can continue evaluating the formula on paper, but the output has stopped representing feasible storage under the stated conditions. A capacity constraint does not invalidate exponentiation. It invalidates using that unconstrained rule as a complete account of the archive.

turns.t: Likewise, an apparent exponential decline may have a floor. Suppose a device's measured signal consists of a decaying component plus a constant background. The decaying component can halve repeatedly while the total reading approaches the background level instead of zero. Taking the logarithm of the total will not generally produce the straight line expected from the isolated exponential component. You would need a justified background estimate before transforming the difference. Subtracting an arbitrary number merely to straighten a graph would change the evidence rather than explain it.

turns.t: Rounding provides another practical complication. If we round a modeled amount to the nearest whole unit after every interval, those rounded values feed into later calculations and can alter the endpoint. Keeping full precision internally and rounding only the reported result avoids that accumulation when the model is continuous. If the actual process genuinely rounds after every step, then that rounding belongs in the model. A numerical convenience and a physical rule are different things, even if both appear as a rounded number in a spreadsheet.

turns.t: For large exponents, logarithms can also keep calculations manageable. Instead of multiplying many huge factors directly, add their logarithms and interpret the result. A base-ten logarithm of six means a factor of one million; a value between six and seven corresponds to a factor between one million and ten million. This is connected to scientific notation, which separates a manageable leading number from a power of ten. It allows us to discuss orders of magnitude without writing a long string of digits or pretending that every digit is meaningful.

turns.t: Take an exact mathematical quantity equal to three times ten to the sixth power. Its base-ten logarithm is six plus the logarithm of three, approximately six point four seven seven. The integer part tells us which neighboring powers of ten surround it. The fractional part locates it within that multiplicative interval. A logarithm of six point five would correspond to the square root of ten times one million, approximately three point one six two million. Halfway up a logarithmic interval is the geometric midpoint, not the ordinary arithmetic midpoint.

turns.t: That gives a sharp chart-reading example. Between ten and one hundred, the arithmetic midpoint is fifty-five. The logarithmic midpoint is the square root of one thousand, approximately thirty-one point six two. The ratios from ten to that midpoint and from that midpoint to one hundred are equal. Each is the square root of ten. Equal distances on a logarithmic scale encode equal multiplication factors, which is why the midpoint differs. A graph can look symmetrical while the underlying absolute distances are unequal.

Keep the unrounded values during calculation. Then compare both the differences and the ratios between successive rows. No personal financial information or real purchasing decision is needed.

Its month-three amount becomes two hundred and seventy-seven point seven two five, and month four becomes about two hundred and ninety-one point six one one. Writing the factor beside each interval makes the changed assumption visible and prevents a smooth-looking formula from hiding it.

The examples and calculations here are original. The core operations now fit together: a fixed addition gives equal differences, a fixed multiplier gives equal ratios, an exponent counts repeated factors, and a logarithm recovers the exponent. A growth factor tells us how a quantity changes; a time interval tells us how often. Once those are specified, doubling, decay, thresholds and equivalent rates become questions we can calculate rather than guess.
